children.text: Dr. Mike uses the affordances of Instagram's text-based captioning features to express his deep frustration with the American healthcare system. The pictorial nature of emoji is an intentional use of social-media captioning capabilities employed by Dr. Mike to express not merely a frustration expressible in words, but one that goes beyond them—one that must be described with pure, unambiguous frustration. Dr. Mike even goes so far as to use the profane dysphemism “Shitty” to modify the noun “Healthcare system,” emphasizing his colossal frustration. For an audience quickly scrolling through the endless abyss of Instagram reels, perhaps occasionally presented with relatively mundane wellness content from Dr. Mike, the enraged visual hook of “ 😡” in this caption, paired with profanity, sourced from Dr. Mike, a brandedly optimistic, kind, and family-centric doctor, emphasizes the immense importance of the problematic American healthcare system—perhaps something worth staying for and watching.

In an attempt to engage a typical viewer of Instagram content, Dr. Mike’s clip takes advantage of an Ab Abrupto rhetorical structure to place the viewer in the middle of an illustrative anecdote. There is no introductory setup or preliminary question to set up the story; instead, while scrolling through the endless chasm of Instagram content, the rhetorical choice to place the viewer immediately into a dependent clause of a dramatic exemplum is a deliberate appeal to the core Aristotelian concept of persuasion: pathos. More specifically, the rhetorical choice to start with “Cause if someone fainted here today, we’re all calling 911” appeals to human curiosity, intrigue, and drama, as well as an innate response to danger, because of how “911” carries an important, intense connotation. The reel itself clearly stems from a longer video, but the dramatic example describing a crisis and the ethical obligations of healthcare professionals is an immediate hook that immerses the viewer in the content and aims to keep them engaged; with this bit as a clip-farmed moment from his longer videos, tailored to perform well in short-form.

Dr. Mike takes advantage of the affordances of video editing tools and, as is common on Instagram, adds overlaid captions to his videos to emphasize key ideas for his audience that are of considerable rhetorical importance relative to other points. Despite the video's predominantly bold white captions, in the middle of Dr. Mike’s story about a child with cancer, he uses the italicized yellow phrase "Make-A-Wish." This color change, juxtaposed with the consistent use of white text, invites the audience to use the captions not merely as a visual aid but as a form of rhetoric and exaggeration in their own right. Yellow, specifically, being the most visible color in the light spectrum to the human eye, triggers a neuroscience principle known as selective attention, which is empirically known to trigger a pathos—including attention and empathy—as Make-A-Wish is often associated with near-death children—the most innocent individuals enduring the most insufferable pain. The goal is to draw the viewer back into the video, given that attention span may be a constraint; in response, Make-A-Wish is associated with heartbreaking events, and yellow text triggers selective attention.

Dr. Mike uses enumeration to emphasize the rigor and emotional cost of being a medical professional, then juxtaposes that intensity with apathy toward financial compensation—thereby establishing an ethos that portrays himself, and doctors generally, as morally altruistic individuals. Through another anecdote, Dr. Mike describes, in succession, a crisis in which he experienced not one, not two, but three medical emergencies back-to-back, then uses hypophora—“Do I need money for that?”— asking a rhetorical question and immediately answering it with “I couldn’t care less.” As an audience member, conceptualizing the tragedy of three simultaneous medical emergencies, the prospect that a doctor thinks of the patient first and finances last builds a sense of trust and credibility. In fact, money isn't even on their list of duties; it's a brief afterthought after an exhaustive list of other obligations doctors choose to endure in the pursuit of helping humanity.

In an attempt to argue that the flaws in the healthcare system that lead to undue stress on healthcare officials stem from the system that sets them up, Dr. Mike appeals to logos, though he seems to commit noticeable logical fallacies. In his conversation with this other individual, Dr. Mike sets up an argument expressing that medical professionals gaslight, fail, and neglect patients. He then attributes the cause to “the system.” Indeed, gaslighting, neglect, and ineffective doctoring are serious issues in healthcare; Dr. Mike, though, seems to be committing a causal oversimplification: quite frequently, ineffective doctoring is a result of the doctor, not the system—or perhaps a doctor unwilling to prioritize patients over the system. Alternatively, he appears to attempt a scapegoating fallacy by arguing that the tension between professionals and hospital administrators is the source of these ethical issues. These issues — like gaslighting — are relatable, frustrating, and key attention-grabbing terms for the video’s audience, and although there is validity to Dr. Mike's argument that the healthcare system is flawed and often leads to clinician burnout, moral distress, and poor quality of care (which, as terms, may not be as algorithmically interesting as gaslighting), the reality is that healthcare is much more complicated than just “the system,” even if it is easier to blame it as a common enemy.

This moment is truly where the exigence of the entire clip comes into play—the fact that politicians are prioritizing relatively unimportant matters in the context of Dr. Mike's profession, while doctors are struggling to afford to live, and corporatization of healthcare continues to dominate, and executives continue to get paid more. Dr. Mike emphasizes this exigence by utilizing a structural parallelism to show that healthcare spending is at an all-time high, while doctor spending is not. The use of "absolutely true" for whether healthcare spending has increased, juxtaposed with "absolutely not" for doctor pay increases, is a direct antithesis that highlights the sharp contrast between higher spending and the lack of corresponding benefits for the individuals who actually enable healthcare systems to operate. Dr. Mike uses hypophora for dramatic effect to deliver the blunt, short truth—that administrators are getting paid exponentially more, while doctors continue to get squeezed. No more fluff is needed to get that point across, and for the audience, the point is presented concisely and clearly.

At the end of the video, Dr. Mike appears to use ragebait-adjacent phrasing to incite frustration among his audience about the political and economic landscape of healthcare and governmental regulation. He argues that Secretary Kennedy calls Dr. Mike a “Profit Monger” and rhetorically asks the individual on camera with him, “Doesn’t that make you angry?” Dr. Mike is laying the groundwork for his audience to become outraged alongside him, others likely frustrated with the healthcare system, perhaps by Secretary Kennedy's aim to unsubstantiatedly defame Tylenol as used by pregnant women or to reduce vaccination requirements, topics Dr. Mike has covered. As a result, Dr. Mike begins vilifying the individual that he argued did the same to him. In this way, Dr. Mike is also creating a false dilemma to incite outrage within his audience. By arguing that Secretary Kennedy is spending his time calling out Dr. Mike, he seems to imply that Secretary Kennedy can’t prioritize other issues within the healthcare system. The ethical issue is that those who trust Dr. Mike as a credible individual may not think deeply about this committed fallacy and emerge outraged at Secretary Kennedy, not for actual missteps, but for personal feuds.
